analysis.one_liner: Overrules state laws that ban city-owned broadband networks from offering service.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in August 2007 but never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Many states have laws, backed by incumbent cable and telephone companies, that bar cities and towns from building or running their own broadband networks. This bill would say no state or local law can prohibit a 'public provider' — a city, town, or state agency — from offering advanced communications service to anyone. To address objections, it adds safeguards: the public network would have to follow the same rules as private competitors, and it would have to publish its plans and hold a public comment process before building. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its telecommunications subcommittee and never went further.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities where private broadband companies have not built service or charge high prices — the bill would let their local governments fill the gap, even in states with bans. It would also help smaller cities negotiate better private service, since a credible public alternative changes what private providers can charge.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any state or local law from prohibiting, or having the effect of prohibiting, a public provider from offering advanced communications capability or services to any person or entity.

Requires public providers to follow the same ordinances, rules, and policies as private providers — including rights-of-way use, permitting, performance bonding, and procurement — so they cannot give themselves a regulatory advantage.

Requires a public provider to publish notice, describe the proposed coverage area and any service to low-income areas, and give local citizens and private-sector entities an opportunity to be heard on costs, benefits, and alternatives before building.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent broadband providers would face new public competitors, which could lower their revenue in areas where cities build. Local taxpayers bear the risk if a city-run network is poorly planned or underused, since public projects are ultimately funded by local government.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent broadband providers and local taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state and local laws through federal preemption, taking the decision away from state legislatures that chose to restrict municipal networks — a significant shift of power to Washington and to city governments.
Public networks are funded by local taxpayers, so a poorly planned or underused municipal network would leave a city covering the losses — a real risk in any government-run utility venture.
The bill could discourage private broadband investment in cities seen as potential public competitors, which could leave residents worse off if the public project never materializes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: in places where private providers will not build or charge high prices, a public option is often the only way to get service, and the bill's safeguards (same rules as private firms, public notice and hearings) are genuine concessions to the opposition. The costs are honest ones — taxpayer risk on public projects and a federalism objection to overriding state law — but they are the price of any public option, not a reason the bill is badly designed. The bill's failure to move was about committee inaction, not its terms.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its telecommunications subcommittee from August 2007 until Congress ended in January 2009, never getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Boucher, a Democrat from Virginia, introduced the bill on August 1, 2007, joined by Rep. Fred Upton, a Republican from Michigan.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet.
No further action was taken — no markup, no hearing result, no floor vote — before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband providers, who benefit from state bans on municipal competition, are better off because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat and a Republican introduced it, with 4 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors — and it died quietly in committee rather than in a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Cable, telephone, and other incumbent broadband providers
industries.note: The bill would void the state laws these companies supported that block city-owned networks from competing with them. Where a public network is built, incumbents would face a competitor able to serve areas they decline to cover, typically at lower prices.
The bill would restore their authority to build and operate broadband networks where state bans currently prevent it, letting them offer service directly to residents.
